# Lighting Control System with Marker-Based Overlay Alignment

## System Overview

The system centers on a user device equipped with several key components that work in concert to provide intuitive control over a specialized lamp. The device includes a display for presenting visual information to the user, a communication interface configured to establish a connection with a lamp that houses multiple individually controllable light sources, and a processor that executes a dedicated software application. This application serves as the central intelligence of the system, coordinating communication with the lamp and managing the user interface.

## Controlling the Source Light Pattern

Through the communication interface, the application directs the lamp to emit light in accordance with a defined source light pattern. This pattern specifies the output characteristics of each individual light source within the lamp, determining how each contributes to the overall illumination. Critically, the source light pattern also designates at least one of the light sources as a marker light source. These marker sources serve a special function within the system, acting as reference points that will later facilitate spatial alignment and control.

## Capturing and Displaying the Projected Pattern

When the lamp projects the source light pattern onto a target surface, the resulting illumination—referred to as the target light pattern—is captured by a camera. Because the target surface may be positioned at an angle, curved, or otherwise oriented relative to the lamp, the projected pattern typically appears distorted rather than as a faithful reproduction of the original source pattern. The user device receives this camera-captured image and presents it on the display, allowing the user to view the actual real-world result of the projected lighting.

## Detecting Marker Locations

To compensate for the distortion inherent in the projected image, the application analyzes the displayed image to detect the positions of the marker light sources. Specifically, it identifies the locations within the image where the designated marker light sources are positioned or where they are intended to emit light onto the target surface. These detected marker positions provide the application with reliable spatial reference points that correspond to known elements of the original source light pattern.

## Aligning the Control Overlay

Using the detected marker locations, the application aligns a control overlay over the displayed image. This alignment maps the overlay accurately onto the distorted target light pattern, ensuring that each element of the overlay corresponds correctly to the real-world position of its associated light source. The overlay identifies the intended area of each individual light source, effectively translating the physical projection into an interactive interface. As a result, the user can control the light sources directly through selections made on the display—adjusting, activating, or otherwise manipulating specific light sources by interacting with the corresponding regions of the aligned overlay.

## Summary

By leveraging designated marker light sources as spatial references, the system overcomes the challenge of projection distortion and provides the user with an intuitive, image-based method for controlling complex lighting arrangements. The combination of accurate marker detection and overlay alignment enables precise, user-friendly control over each light source relative to its actual appearance on the target surface.

# Intuitive Light Source Control Through Camera-Based Pattern Recognition

## System Overview

A user device—such as a smartphone or tablet equipped with both a display screen and an integrated camera—runs a dedicated software application designed to interface with and control a lamp containing multiple individual light sources. Rather than requiring users to manually identify and address each light source through abstract controls, the system leverages visual recognition technology to create an intuitive, spatially-aware control interface.

## Establishing the Source Light Pattern

When the application is activated, it instructs the lamp to illuminate its multiple light sources according to a predetermined source light pattern. Within this pattern, certain light sources are designated as **marker light sources**. These markers serve as reference points that the system can later recognize and use for spatial calibration. The remaining light sources fill out the pattern in known positions relative to these markers.

## Capturing the Projected Image

As the lamp projects this light pattern onto a target surface—such as a wall, ceiling, or table—the user directs their device's camera toward the illuminated area. Because the camera is rarely positioned perpendicular to the surface, and because the projection geometry varies with distance and angle, the captured image typically appears **distorted**. The pattern may look skewed, stretched, or rotated compared to its original configuration. This distorted image is then rendered on the device's display for the user to see.

## Detecting Markers and Aligning the Overlay

The core of the system's intelligence lies in its ability to detect the locations of the marker light sources within the displayed image. By identifying where these known reference points appear in the distorted view, the application can mathematically determine how the entire pattern has been transformed by the projection and viewing angle. Using this information, the system aligns a **control overlay** onto the displayed image. This overlay maps each individual light source to the specific area it occupies within the projected image, accurately accounting for any distortion.

## Enabling Intuitive User Control

With the control overlay properly aligned, the user can now interact directly with the light sources as they appear on the display. By tapping or selecting a particular region of the projected pattern shown on screen, the user issues commands to the corresponding physical light source in the lamp. This creates a natural, direct-manipulation experience: users control lights simply by touching where those lights appear in the real-world projection, eliminating the need to guess which control corresponds to which light source and making the entire system remarkably intuitive to operate.

# A User Device

A user device is any piece of hardware or equipment that an individual uses to access, interact with, and communicate through digital systems, networks, or services. These devices serve as the primary interface between people and the vast world of technology, enabling everything from simple communication to complex computing tasks.

## Common Types of User Devices

User devices come in many forms, each designed to serve specific needs:

- **Smartphones** – Perhaps the most widely used device today, combining communication, computing, and multimedia capabilities in a portable form.
- **Laptops and Desktops** – Traditional computing devices used for work, education, gaming, and content creation.
- **Tablets** – Portable touchscreen devices that bridge the gap between smartphones and laptops.
- **Wearables** – Smartwatches and fitness trackers that monitor health and provide quick access to notifications.
- **Smart TVs and Set-Top Boxes** – Devices that connect to the internet for streaming and entertainment.

## Key Characteristics

A typical user device includes several essential components:

1. **Input methods** – Such as keyboards, touchscreens, microphones, or cameras that allow users to provide commands.
2. **Output methods** – Displays, speakers, or haptic feedback that deliver information back to the user.
3. **Processing power** – Internal hardware that runs software and applications.
4. **Connectivity** – Wi-Fi, cellular data, or Bluetooth that link the device to networks and other devices.

## Importance in Modern Life

User devices have become deeply integrated into daily activities. They enable remote work, online learning, digital banking, entertainment, and social connection. As technology advances, these devices continue to become more powerful, portable, and interconnected, shaping how people live, work, and communicate.

## Security Considerations

Because user devices often store sensitive personal information, protecting them is crucial. Common security practices include using strong passwords, enabling encryption, keeping software updated, and being cautious about the applications and networks a device connects to.

In summary, a user device is a fundamental tool in the digital age, empowering individuals to access information and services while requiring responsible use and protection.

**Claim 1.** A user device for controlling a lamp comprising a plurality of light sources, the user device comprising:

a camera configured to capture an image of the lamp;

a display; and

a processor operatively coupled to the camera and the display, the processor being configured to:

    identify, in the captured image, at least two marker light sources of the plurality of light sources;

    determine, based on respective positions of the identified marker light sources within the captured image, an alignment of a control overlay relative to the captured image;

    render, on the display, the control overlay aligned in accordance with the determined alignment, the control overlay comprising one or more control elements each associated with a respective one of the plurality of light sources;

    receive a user input directed to a control element of the control overlay; and

    transmit, in response to the user input, a control signal to the lamp to control the light source associated with the control element to which the user input is directed.

---

*Notes for consideration:*

- **Marker identification:** You may wish to add a dependent claim specifying that the marker light sources emit a distinguishable characteristic (e.g., a predetermined color, modulation pattern, or temporal sequence) to enable identification and disambiguation from other light sources.
- **Overlay alignment:** Consider a dependent claim covering perspective/scale correction of the overlay based on the relative geometry (distance, angle) of the marker light sources.
- **Breadth:** The term "user device" is deliberately broad to capture a smartphone, tablet, AR headset, etc. Confirm this aligns with your intended scope and prior-art landscape.
- **Two-way vs. one-way:** If the device also receives status/feedback from the lamp, an additional independent or dependent claim may be warranted.

This is a drafting aid and not legal advice; a qualified patent attorney should review claim scope against your invention disclosure and relevant prior art before filing.

counterfactuals.output:
# Patent Claim: Marker Light Source Detection and Lighting Control Alignment Device

## Independent Claim

**1.** A device comprising:

a display configured to present a graphical user interface;

a camera interface configured to receive image data from at least one camera, said image data comprising one or more frames captured of a physical environment; and

a processor operatively coupled to the display and the camera interface, said processor configured to execute an application, wherein the application, when executed, causes the processor to:

**(a)** receive, via the camera interface, at least one frame of said image data representing a physical environment containing one or more marker light sources, each marker light source emitting a detectable optical signal;

**(b)** analyze the at least one frame to detect a respective location of each of the one or more marker light sources within a coordinate space of the frame, wherein detecting the respective location comprises identifying, within the image data, one or more pixel regions exhibiting an intensity characteristic exceeding a predetermined threshold associated with said detectable optical signal;

**(c)** determine, based on the detected respective location of each marker light source, a spatial mapping between the coordinate space of the frame and a control coordinate space of a lighting control overlay;

**(d)** generate the lighting control overlay comprising one or more interactive control elements, each interactive control element being associated with a respective one of the one or more marker light sources; and

**(e)** render, on the display, the lighting control overlay superimposed upon the at least one frame such that each interactive control element is aligned, according to said spatial mapping, with the detected respective location of its associated marker light source.

---

## Dependent Claims

**2.** The device of claim 1, wherein the detectable optical signal comprises a modulated light signal encoding an identifier, and wherein the application further causes the processor to decode said identifier to associate each detected marker light source with a corresponding controllable lighting fixture.

**3.** The device of claim 2, wherein the modulated light signal comprises a temporal modulation pattern detectable across a plurality of successive frames of said image data.

**4.** The device of claim 1, wherein the intensity characteristic comprises at least one of a luminance value, a chrominance value, or a spectral signature corresponding to a wavelength emitted by the marker light source.

**5.** The device of claim 1, wherein the application further causes the processor to:

track the respective location of each marker light source across a plurality of successive frames; and

dynamically update the alignment of each interactive control element in response to relative motion between the camera and the one or more marker light sources.

**6.** The device of claim 1, wherein each interactive control element is configured to receive a user input via the display, and wherein the application further causes the processor to transmit, in response to said user input, a control command to a lighting fixture associated with the corresponding marker light source.

**7.** The device of claim 6, wherein the control command adjusts at least one of a brightness, a color, a color temperature, or a power state of the associated lighting fixture.

**8.** The device of claim 1, wherein the spatial mapping comprises a geometric transformation accounting for at least one of a perspective distortion, a rotation, a scaling, or a translation between the coordinate space of the frame and the control coordinate space.

**9.** The device of claim 1, wherein the application further causes the processor to distinguish the one or more marker light sources from ambient light sources by applying a filtering operation based on at least one of a predetermined spectral band, a predetermined modulation frequency, or a predetermined spatial extent.

**10.** The device of claim 1, wherein the display comprises a touchscreen, and wherein the graphical user interface is configured to receive touch input directed to the interactive control elements of the lighting control overlay.

**11.** The device of claim 1, wherein the one or more marker light sources comprise infrared emitters, and wherein the at least one camera comprises a sensor sensitive to infrared wavelengths.

**12.** The device of claim 1, wherein the application further causes the processor to display, when a marker light source is detected to be outside a field of view of the camera, a directional indicator on the display guiding a user to reorient the camera toward said marker light source.

**13.** The device of claim 1, wherein the device comprises one of a smartphone, a tablet computer, a head-mounted display, or augmented reality glasses.

**14.** The device of claim 1, wherein the application further causes the processor to:

detect a plurality of marker light sources associated with a lighting group; and

generate a group control element within the lighting control overlay operable to simultaneously control all lighting fixtures associated with the lighting group.

**15.** The device of claim 1, wherein the application further causes the processor to store, in a memory, a persistent association between each detected marker light source and a user-defined label, said user-defined label being rendered proximate to the corresponding interactive control element in the lighting control overlay.

---

*Note: This claim set is provided as a drafting example for illustrative purposes. A qualified patent attorney or agent should review and adapt any claims prior to filing, including conducting a prior art search and ensuring compliance with applicable patentability requirements.*

**What is claimed is:**

**1.** A user device comprising:

a lamp configured to emit a source light pattern onto a surface;

a plurality of marker light sources configured to emit reference indicia detectable within the captured projected light pattern; and
